appreciate: Thank you for the lovely scarf, I really appreciate it.
I appreciate the sunshine after so many grey, rainy days!
We say thank you because we appreciate the cake you baked.
attached: The kite string is firmly attached to the wooden handle.
Is the tag still attached to your new coat?
Look how the little shell is attached to the rock!
communicate: Gran lives far away, so we communicate by video call every Sunday.
Dolphins use clicks and whistles to communicate with each other.
How do you communicate with friends who speak another language?
exaggerate: It was only a drizzle, so don't exaggerate and say it poured!
My brother caught a tiny fish but likes to exaggerate its size.
Does she exaggerate when she says her small kitten is huge?
equip: Mum plans to equip our garden shed with shelves and hooks.
Will the teacher equip each group with scissors and glue?
Let's equip the new den with cushions, torches and snacks!
equipped: Dad equipped the shed with new shelves last weekend.
Is the kitchen equipped with a big oven and a fridge?
The explorers felt well equipped, with maps, snacks and warm hats!
equipment: Please put the sports equipment back in the cupboard.
Which equipment do we need for the science lesson?
The gardener keeps her tools and other equipment in a shed.
interrupt: Please wait your turn and do not interrupt your friend's story.
Sorry to interrupt, but dinner is ready!
Will the rain interrupt our picnic this afternoon?
interfere: Please do not interfere with my model while the glue dries.
Loud music may interfere with my homework.
Thick clouds can interfere with the view of the stars.
suggest: Can anyone suggest a name for our class hamster?
I suggest we take our umbrellas because of the dark clouds.
The librarian will suggest a good book if you ask her.

rejected.s: We all appreciate how hard the dinner ladies work every day.
rejected.reason: checker: 'We all exaggerate how hard...' also works in the gap, and 'dinner ladies' leans on a gender stereotype. (also fits: exaggerate)

rejected.s: Do you appreciate the kind things your friends do for you?
rejected.reason: checker: 'Do you exaggerate the kind things...' also makes sense. (also fits: exaggerate)

rejected.s: The class wrote a thank you card to appreciate the helpful librarian.
rejected.reason: checker: 'To appreciate the librarian' sounds unnatural; we would say 'to thank'.

rejected.s: The trailer was attached to the back of the tractor.
rejected.reason: machine rule 5: shares a run of 4 words with the example

rejected.s: Saying the queue was a mile long would exaggerate a little.
rejected.reason: checker: The grammar is awkward; it should be 'would be exaggerating'.

rejected.s: Did the fish really weigh a ton, or do you exaggerate?
rejected.reason: checker: The tense is wrong; it should be 'are you exaggerating', so it reads unnaturally.

rejected.s: I don't want to exaggerate, but this is the best cake ever!
rejected.reason: checker: 'I don't want to interrupt, but...' also makes good sense. (also fits: interrupt, interfere)

rejected.s: It is rude to interrupt when your teacher is talking.
rejected.reason: checker: 'It is rude to interfere' also makes sense here. (also fits: interfere)

rejected.s: If the puppy tries to interfere, the wool will get tangled.
rejected.reason: checker: 'If the puppy tries to interrupt' also works in the gap. (also fits: interrupt)

rejected.s: Mum drove us to school in the rain, so we appreciate the lift.
rejected.reason: checker: Moving from past 'drove' to present 'appreciate' sounds awkward, so the sentence is not natural.

rejected.s: Do you appreciate a warm drink after a cold walk home?
rejected.reason: checker: 'Do you suggest a warm drink after a cold walk home?' also makes sense. (also fits: suggest)

rejected.s: How much I appreciate a cosy bed after a long journey!
rejected.reason: checker: This old-fashioned exclamation is hard for a Year 5 child to read naturally.

rejected.s: Waiting ten minutes is not hours, so please do not exaggerate!
rejected.reason: checker: 'Waiting ten minutes is not hours' is awkward English for a child.
